paras: The attempted lynching of D. R. Stokes took place on the night of February 25, 1903, in Gregg County, Texas, when a large body of white men seized Stokes, a Black preacher from Dallas who had been speaking against prohibition, and prepared to hang him across the Sabine River. By Stokes's account, he was spared after he made the Masonic sign of distress and a white leader who had urged the lynching demanded his life, on condition that he never return to the county. The story became public about two weeks later through a federal official in Dallas and ran in white dailies across the country and in two Black weeklies, chiefly as a tale of a life saved by Freemasonry.

Stokes was described in the dispatches as "the most prominent negro preacher and educator in Dallas." He said he had been hired to make speeches against prohibition and had been campaigning vigorously among Black voters in Gregg County, urging them to vote against it. Two versions of the dispatch added that Gregg County went strongly for prohibition in the election, which the Cleveland Gazette's text placed ten days before the report.

In the midst of a speech, a large body of white men rushed into the meeting and seized him. They took him to the Sabine River, rowed him to the other side and prepared to hang him. Hoping his standing in Freemasonry would help, Stokes made the Masonic sign of distress.

Almost at once a white man who appeared to be a leader, and who had been among the strongest advocates of lynching him, stepped to his side and demanded that his life be spared. In the shorter wire text the man instead "begged for his life." He gave the others no reason for his change of mind but said, "Spare him and I will guarantee that he never again sets foot in Gregg county." The crowd consented, and the white man hurried Stokes out of the county; Stokes said he had not been back and never intended to return.

Stokes later reported the attack to W. H. Atwell, a federal official at Dallas called both United States marshal and United States attorney. Atwell was reported to have investigated the story and found it true. He said he knew of no law allowing a federal prosecution, and Stokes did not want one. Both men refused to give the name of the white man who had saved Stokes, and no report of a state or local investigation or of any arrest appears in the coverage.

The story went out as a Dallas dispatch dated March 12, and that day the Rock Island Argus headed it "Saved from Lynching by a Masonic Charm" while the Washington Times used "Saved from Lynching by a Masonic Sign." The same text ran with later datelines in the Waterbury Evening Democrat on March 13 under "Sign Stopped Lynching" and in the Wheeling Sunday Register on March 15. A fuller version, carried by the Daily Ardmoreite on March 13 under "Badly Scared" and by the Raleigh News and Observer on March 20 as a special to the New York Times, added Atwell's remark that no federal law applied.

The white papers called Stokes a "negro preacher" and his attackers "white men" or "a band of white prohibitionists," without comment. The one editorial notice, in the Savannah Morning News, retold it as "an odd and interesting if true story" and attributed the Masonic sign to Stokes's own word.

In the Black press, the Cleveland Gazette reprinted the dispatch on March 21 in its Dayton, Ohio, column under the headline "Saved From It by the Mystic Signal of Distress When About to be Lynched." Its text called Stokes "Rev. Dr. Stokes" and an "Afro-American" minister, and where the white papers wrote "white men" it wrote "white brutes." The Professional World printed the short Dallas item on March 27 without comment, keeping the wire's statement that the attack came because Stokes had urged Black voters to oppose prohibition.
Every version rests on Stokes's own statement, which Atwell was reported to have confirmed, and no account from Gregg County or from the men involved appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of D. R. Stokes
bases: A large body of white men seized Stokes at a meeting, took him across the Sabine River and prepared to hang him, but released him alive (A3, A4, A8).

A 'large body of white men' acting without legal authority prepared to hang Stokes but spared him, so no one was killed (A3, A4, A8); this was an attempted lynching, and the stated reason was his speeches against prohibition rather than an accusation of crime (A1, A10).

Every report, white and Black, derives from Stokes's own statement relayed in Dallas dispatches (A3, A4, A8, A9, A10); Atwell was reported to have investigated and confirmed it (A3, A8), but no independent local or eyewitness account appears, and the Savannah Morning News called it true only 'if' (A6).

framing.detail: Headlines 'Saved from Lynching by a Masonic Charm' and 'Saved from Lynching by a Masonic Sign' made the Masonic rescue the story; the attackers were 'a band of white prohibitionists'.
The Daily Ardmoreite headed it 'Badly Scared. A Negro Preacher Who Made Prohibition Speeches Had a Fright.'
The Savannah Morning News called it 'an odd and interesting if true story' and called the attackers 'a mob of white men'.
The News & Observer ran the New York Times special under 'Masonic Sign Saved Him', adding that Gregg county went strongly for prohibition.
The Cleveland Gazette's reprint called Stokes an 'Afro-American' minister and the attackers 'white brutes', under 'Saved From It by the Mystic Signal of Distress'.
The Professional World printed the short Dallas wire item without comment.
